name: Blood Pressure

yellow.text: Top number 121–139 or bottom 81–89 (high); top 86–99 or bottom 56–59 (low)

red.text: 140/90 or higher; 85/55 or lower; or any reading with fainting or chest pain

equipment: Strap or tether to hold the arm in place
steps: Rest quietly for a few minutes. Do not drink coffee or exercise first.
Fit the cuff on your bare upper arm and strap the arm at heart level so it does not float.
Press start, stay still and silent, then record both numbers.
when: Daily within 30 minutes of waking, before caffeine or exercise, and never within 45 minutes after an ARED workout.
mistakes: Measuring within 45 minutes of an ARED workout.
Letting the arm float away from heart level.
Talking or moving during the reading.
Comparing with Earth values only: your space baseline sits slightly lower.
escalate_if: The reading is Yellow or Red after a 30-minute seated rest and repeat.
Any dizziness, fainting or chest pain: tick the symptom checklist.
why: In weightlessness body fluid shifts toward the head and blood volume falls by 12–15%, so a healthy astronaut's blood pressure sits a little below Earth averages. Readings that drift out of your own band can mean volume loss or strain on the heart and vessels.
benefits: Spots dehydration or heart strain early.
Uses your adapted baseline, so normal space changes do not cause false alarms.
Pairs with resting heart rate on the same node.

yellow: Sit and rest for 30 minutes, then repeat the measurement.
Check resting heart rate (1A-ii) and hydration.
Follow the crew medical checklist for fluid loading if the reading is low.
red: Repeat after 30 minutes of seated rest.
Avoid exertion and EVA until cleared.
Include the 7-day trend in the report packet.

name: Resting Heart Rate

red.text: Over 100 bpm at rest on 2 readings 10 minutes apart, under 40 bpm, or with symptoms

equipment: Pulse oximeter, wrist band or chest strap that shows heart rate
Same device as the blood pressure cuff if it reads pulse
steps: Stay seated or strapped in, relaxed and still, for a few minutes.
Start the reading with the cuff, band or strap.
Record the steady number, not the first one that appears.
when: Daily, at the same time as the waking blood pressure.
mistakes: Measuring right after movement or exercise.
Reading the first flicker of the display instead of the steady value.
Using the Earth range instead of your own baseline.
Skipping the second reading when the first is over 100.
escalate_if: Over 100 bpm on 2 readings 10 minutes apart.
Any fainting, chest pain or dizziness.
why: Heart rate shows how the heart is coping with fluid shifts and lower blood volume. A rise or a drop from your own baseline can signal dehydration, illness or stress on the autonomic nervous system.

yellow: Rest 10 minutes, drink water and repeat.
Measure twice a day until it returns to Green.
red: Repeat after 10 minutes of rest to confirm.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer and send the trend in the report packet.

name: Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter (ONSD)

earth_range.text: 4.2–5.0 mm (5.9 mm or more is abnormal on Earth)

red.text: 5.8 mm or more, or any new blurred vision or lasting headache

steps: Close the eye, cover it with gel and rest the probe gently on the eyelid. Do not press.
Find the optic nerve behind the eye and freeze the image in the axial plane.
Measure the width of the dark sheath exactly 3 mm behind the back of the eye, and record it.
when: Every 3 days (demo schedule). Repeat in 24 hours if Yellow.
mistakes: Pressing on the eyelid, which squeezes the sheath.
Measuring at the wrong distance behind the eye (it must be 3 mm).
Using the Earth cutoff of 5.9 mm: your space alert starts earlier.
Taking one reading and ignoring the trend.
escalate_if: New blurred vision or a headache that does not go away.
why: Without gravity, fluid and pressure build up around the head. The optic nerve sheath widens, and this can lead to Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). ONSD is a screening sign, not a diagnosis, so a high value needs an expert to review the images.
benefits: Early warning for vision-threatening pressure changes.
Lets the flight surgeon see the trend before symptoms start.
Prompts a check of cabin CO₂, which can make it worse.

red: Remember ONSD is a screen, not a diagnosis.
Send the ultrasound and any eye images to the flight surgeon (store-and-forward).
Schedule lower-body negative pressure per the crew medical checklist.

name: 24-hour Urine Calcium

input.label: 24-hour urine calcium (typed from the lab result)

steps: Collect all urine for 24 hours in the collection container.
Run the sample on the analyzer and read the calcium result.
Type the value (mg/day) into the check-in.
when: Weekly as a full 24-hour test. A hydration strip can be checked daily.
mistakes: Thinking a hydration strip photo measures calcium. It only shows hydration.
Starting the 24 hours at a different time than the log says.
escalate_if: Flank pain, blood in urine or a lot less urine.
why: Bones lose calcium in weightlessness, and it passes out in the urine. Together with lower urine volume, this makes kidney stones more likely, which could be a mission-ending emergency far from Earth.
benefits: Tracks bone loss and stone risk.
Shows whether exercise and hydration are working.
Gives the flight surgeon numbers to adjust treatment.

yellow: Drink about 1 extra litre of water gradually over several hours.
Review vitamin D and sodium intake (salt raises calcium loss).
Ask the flight surgeon whether treatment is needed.
red: Tell the Crew Medical Officer and send the result to the flight surgeon.
Follow flight-surgeon direction on any treatment, such as potassium citrate.
